jsnvu6-e180864-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 7: whether the act of faith is more certain than the act of science, or the reverse, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e117.summary: Argument that faith is more certain: acts relate as their habits, and Augustine (De Trinitate XIII) says nothing is more certain to a person than his faith.
claims: Faith is more certain than science (objection from Augustine)

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e135.summary: Second argument: knowledge is as certain as the middle causing it, and divine authority, the middle of faith, is more certain than any human reason, the middle of science.
claims: Divine authority is a more certain middle than human reason (objection)

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e152.summary: Argument for the opposite: sight is more certain than hearing, faith comes by hearing (Rom. 10), science is intellectual sight, and some sciences' principles resolve into things seen bodily, as in mathematics.
claims: Science, as intellectual sight, is more certain than faith, which comes by hearing

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e170.summary: Second argument for the opposite: Hugh of St Victor defines faith as voluntary certitude above opinion and below science.
claims: Faith's certitude is below that of science (Hugh of St Victor)

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e181.summary: Outline of the response: first, which of the acts called faith—credere Deum, credere Deo, credere in Deum—is most properly the act of faith; second, the comparison of faith's act with science's.

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e194.summary: First article: credere Deum and credere Deo are precisely acts of faith and one single act; credere in Deum is an act of faith and charity together and so more than one act. God relates to belief in three ways: as object believed (that God is triune, incarnate), as reason or middle of believing (divine truth revealing), and as end (John 20). Credere Deum names the relation to God as object, credere Deo to God as motive; since one act attains object through middle, these are one act. Credere in Deum names relation to God as end shown by faith and sought by charity, meaning to love in believing and tend to him, and so involves two habits.
claims: Credere Deum and credere Deo are one and the same act of faith
Credere in Deum involves both faith and charity and so is not one act
God relates to the act of belief as object, as motive, and as end

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e257.summary: Second article: rejects the view that science excels in certitude of evidence while faith excels in certitude of adherence. Firmness of adherence is improperly called certitude, since it coexists with falsity, as in heretics and the obstinate; and adherence even seems firmer in a genuine knower who knows he knows, since people frequently abandon faith.
claims: Firmness of adherence is not properly certitude, since it can coexist with falsehood
Adherence is firmer in genuine science than in faith, which people often abandon

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e301.summary: Rejects a second view: that belief is more certain in itself (secundum se) and science more certain for us (quoad nos). The distinction may apply to objects (Metaphysics II on separate substances) but not to habits and acts: a habit is a disposition of the knower and an act its perfection relative to the object, so a habit or act is more certain only if it makes the object more certain to us; a nobler object only makes the knowledge nobler. Aristotle's De anima distinguishes nobility by certitude from nobility by object, confirming this.
claims: The secundum se / quoad nos distinction does not apply to the certitude of habits and acts
A habit or act is more certain only insofar as it makes its object more certain to us
Nobility of object and certitude of knowledge are distinct
concepts: certitude secundum se vs. quoad nos

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e361.summary: Digression on the Metaphysics II distinction of what is more known in itself and to us: since known-ness is a relation to a knower, nothing is known absolutely in itself. Properly understood, what is more known to God is more known simply, what is known to angels in the second degree, and what is known to humans, the lowest intellects, least. Higher beings are 'more known in themselves' because God and the angels know them first—God knowing all through his essence—whereas sensibles are first known by us.
claims: Nothing is known in itself absolutely, only relative to some knower
'More known simply' means more known to the highest knowers, God and angels
Humans are the lowest intellectual creatures
concepts: notius secundum se vs. quoad nos

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e429.summary: Durandus's own answer: though some credibles, such as the Trinity, are more certain and known in themselves than many things known of creatures, many habits and acts of science are more certain than faith, both extensively and intensively. Extensively, science has certitude of evidence and of adherence (if adherence is certitude), faith only of adherence. Intensively, science admits no admixture of doubt, whereas faith can, even with faith intact. Moreover, the blessed's knowledge of God is more certain than believers' faith despite the same object, so certitude follows mode not object; likewise our science that God is one is more certain than our faith that God is triune.
claims: Science is more certain than faith both extensively and intensively
Faith can coexist with some admixture of doubt
Certitude depends on the mode of the intellect's tending, not on the object
Knowledge that God is one is more certain than faith that God is triune

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e486.summary: Reply to Augustine: he does not mean that faith certifies its objects as science does, but that a believer is as certain of having faith as of anything, since he experiences himself believing, and nothing is more certain than experience, into which other certitudes resolve.
claims: Augustine means one is certain of possessing faith, not of its objects as in science
Experience is the most certain cognition

jsnvu6-e180864-d1e508.summary: Reply to the second: a more certain middle yields more certain knowledge only if it is more certain to us. Divine authority is most certain in itself but not to us: we know that God says what we believe only because the Church holds it, and we hold by faith alone that Scripture is backed by divine authority. So divine authority is not better known to us than demonstrative reason.
claims: A middle confers certitude only as it is certain to us
We hold by faith alone that Scripture rests on divine authority
Our access to divine authority is mediated by the Church's teaching

jsnvu6-e180864.summary: Question 7 asks whether the act of faith is more certain than the act of science. Durandus first fixes the proper act of faith: credere Deum (God as object) and credere Deo (God as motive or middle) are one and the same act of faith, while credere in Deum, tending to God as end, combines faith and charity. On certitude he rejects two common solutions: that faith excels in certitude of adherence (adherence is not properly certitude, coexists with falsehood, and is in fact firmer in genuine science), and that faith is more certain in itself but science more certain to us (the distinction applies to objects, not to habits or acts, whose certitude is always certitude for us). In a digression he reinterprets 'more known in itself' as more known to higher knowers, God and the angels. His own position is that science is more certain than faith both extensively (evidence plus adherence) and intensively (no admixture of doubt), since certitude follows the mode of cognition, not the object. Augustine means only that one is certain of having faith. Divine authority, though certain in itself, is known to us only through faith and the Church's teaching.
claims: Credere Deum and credere Deo are a single act of faith; credere in Deum includes charity
Firmness of adherence is not certitude properly speaking
Certitude of habits and acts is always relative to the knower
Science is more certain than faith extensively and intensively
Divine authority is not better known to us than demonstrative reason
